articles.title: The memory crisis is killing off sub-$100 smartphones as US sales plunge 64%
articles.text:
Connecting the dots: Buying a smartphone for under $100 could soon become something you used to be able to do. According to the latest sales figures, this segment declined by 64% YoY in the second quarter – and there are no prizes for guessing why.
Counterpoint Research writes that US smartphone sales fell by 5% YoY in Q2 2026, with memory price increases the main culprit alongside other macroeconomic factors weakening consumer demand.
The market research firm writes that rising RAM demand from hyperscalers continues to drive up memory costs. Meanwhile, higher prices for other goods stemming from conflict in the Middle East are reducing consumers' purchasing power for smartphones and other electronics.
The problem is especially bad for smaller brands, several of which, including HMD, have left the US market or downsized operations. As a result, sub-$100 smartphone sales declined 64% as OEMs either stopped shipping these devices or were forced to increase prices to offset increased memory costs.
Carrier-branded white-label phones were among the hardest hit. The jump in component costs has narrowed the price gap between these devices and entry-level handsets from larger manufacturers such as Samsung and Motorola, giving buyers less reason to choose the lesser-known alternatives.
Motorola's price increases have seen its G-series phones moved into the previously sparse $200 – $299 bracket, helping sales in that segment grow by almost 200% YoY and tripling its share of the US market.
The squeeze is unlikely to end in the current quarter. Counterpoint expects average smartphone selling prices to continue rising in Q3, when Apple is also expected to increase prices for its iPhone 18 series. Earlier this year, CEO Tim Cook confirmed that price hikes across Apple's product lineup were becoming unavoidable, while one estimate suggested base iPhones could increase by more than $200. Apple has since raised prices on all of its MacBooks and iPads.
This isn't the first time we've heard of a budget electronics category facing extinction because of the memory crunch. In March, Gartner predicted that the rising cost of RAM and NAND could result in the sub-$500 PC market disappearing by 2028.
It was recently reported that global sales of smartphones costing less than $400 are expected to fall 22% this year. Omdia found that memory represented nearly 60% of the bill of materials for these phones in Q1, rising above 64% for devices priced below $99.

articles.title: Vercel Launches v0 API for Headless App Building
articles.text:
Vercel has made the v0 API generally available, providing programmatic access to its AI-powered application-building agent. Developers can send prompts through the API, have v0 generate and modify application files, run the resulting app in a Vercel Sandbox, and receive a preview URL that can be embedded into their own interfaces.
The API organizes each application around a chat that maintains the app's current state. Developers can send follow-up messages using the same chat ID, allowing v0 to continue editing the existing application. The API supports synchronous, asynchronous, and streaming requests, with streamed responses exposing individual agent actions such as file reads, edits, searches, Bash commands, and tool calls.
Applications can also be created from existing GitHub repositories, ZIP archives, or sets of files. When the app is ready, developers can attach a Vercel project and deploy it through the API. Preview environments use short-lived tokens and can be accessed through a server-side proxy, keeping the v0 API key out of the browser.
The API also supports external tools and design systems. Developers can connect MCP servers or load skills from team or user memory, skills.sh, or a connected repository. Up to three skills can be passed to a request. Vercel also provides integrations for using v0 as a tool inside other AI agents through MCP, the AI SDK, or Vercel's eve framework.
This positions v0 differently from application-building tools such as Lovable and Bolt, which primarily provide interactive environments for generating applications. The v0 API instead exposes the application-building agent as infrastructure that developers can invoke from their own products, scripts, CI pipelines, or other agents. Vercel's approach also integrates the generated application directly with its Sandbox and deployment APIs.
Community reaction has focused on the potential for the API to support fully programmatic application development. AI influencer ZenithAI described the release as:
A powerful step toward fully programmatic app development workflows.
Vercel developer @EstebanSuarez highlighted the intended agent workflow, explaining that an agent can send a prompt and design system to the v0 API, receive a live preview in a Vercel Sandbox, iterate on the application, and deploy it when ready, posting:
Your agent needs an app. It sends a prompt to the v0 API along with your design system. Back comes a preview URL: the app live in a Vercel Sandbox. Your agent iterates on it. When it's ready, it deploys. That's the new v0 API.
The new API is available through the v0 SDK, with the v2 API using https://api.v0.dev/v2. Developers can create an API key, install the SDK, and build interfaces that send prompts, stream agent activity, render previews, and deploy generated applications.

articles.title: Rivian's 2027 changes include its No. 1 most-requested feature
articles.text:
It’s time for Rivian’s changeover from model year 2026 to 2027, and the electric vehicle startup has decided to take a page from its recently released R2 SUV and apply it to the company’s larger, more expensive R1 line. The changes aren’t massive—the R1 got a refresh in 2024 that saw the R1S SUV and R1T pickup each get some comprehensive re-engineering with new powertrain options, a new electronic architecture, and new batteries.
But among them is the No. 1 most requested feature by Rivian R1S customers, the automaker told Ars: captain’s chairs for the second row. The six-seat interior is an alternative to a middle bench, and the Rivian captain’s chair looks thoughtfully designed, with a hidden cupholder that I’m not sure I’ve seen on any other SUV before. The chairs are also spaced so it’s easy to get to the third row, or use that volume between them for skis, snowboards, or surfboards.
Rivian has also changed the trims, bringing them into line with the offer structure on the recently released R2. Instead of choosing from Dual, Tri, or R1s, Rivian is now calling them Premium and Performance; Quad stays Quad. But the base price for each stays the same: The R1T still starts at $79,990 and the R1S at $83,990.

articles.title: Lyon’s AMDB Security Pro locks in €2.68 million to take its excavator anti-theft systems to the US | EU-Startups
articles.text:
AMDB Security Pro, a Lyon-based engineering company providing mechanical anti-theft systems for excavators and mini-excavators, has announced the close of a €2.68 million ($3.1 million) Seed funding round from two American private investors.
The company plans to use this capital to accelerate its establishment in the United States, where it plans to set up a subsidiary, build strategic partnerships, and continue R&D into new equipment categories.
“Closing this round marks a defining step for AMDB Security Pro as we prepare our establishment in the United States. This investment lets us build our U.S. operations, deepen our relationships with rental companies, insurers, and equipment manufacturers, and keep advancing our technology into new equipment categories,” said Pascal Oltra, co-founder of AMDB Security Pro.
Founded by Pascal Oltra and Kevin Kaarouche, AMDB Security Pro claims to have created the first made-in-France mechanical anti-theft system for excavators and mini-excavators: a patented, tamper-resistant device designed to prevent unauthorised machine starts in demanding construction environments.
Highlighting the fact that construction equipment theft is a major, costly problem in the United States, AMDB Security Pro states that its approach involves stopping theft before it happens.
The device is made from hardened boron steel, an ultra-resistant, specialised alloy designed to withstand sawing, bolt-cutter attacks, and twisting attempts. It also features a 120 dB alarm, a GPS tracker, and a discreet compartment for securely storing the key within the anti-theft system. The company notes that its system is compatible with over 100 brands of mini-excavators and construction equipment
The funding round comes as AMDB Security Pro prepares to enter the world’s largest construction equipment and rental market. The capital will fund the company’s U.S. expansion, from opening a subsidiary and hiring its first local teams to a deeper commercial and operational structuring effort aimed at large-scale deployment across the American market by 2027.
As part of its international expansion, AMDB Security Pro will continue serving excavator and mini-excavator operators while extending its engineering approach to a broader range of equipment.

articles.title: Marvel's Wolverine has thrillingly visceral combat, but it's the narrative that's most surprising
articles.text:
Marvel’s Wolverine is a lot.
Throughout my two-hour demo, I carved up scores of soldiers as almost comically large pools of blood sprayed everywhere. I waded through a pile of mutant corpses to confront a genocidal scientist. I died several times to a fearsome Sentinel. I chased a cabal of clandestine ninjas across the rooftops of the neon-soaked fictional Southeast Asian city of Madripoor. And yet, there’s a particular quiet dialogue scene that I keep thinking about weeks after playing Insomniac’s latest superhero game.
After a traumatic event at the end of Act 1, Wolverine and his mutant allies have gathered at the Princess Bar in Madripoor. At their most shaken and vulnerable, it’s an opportunity for “Team X” — Wolverine’s group of operatives that exists in this pre-X-Men universe — to find solace among their found family. It also allows the player, as Logan, to walk around and talk with a bunch of NPCs. But it was Wolverine’s exchange with Mystique, of all people, that’s stuck with me.
Behind the bar, the shapeshifter challenges me to a game of “Never Have I Ever,” and I, as the ever-grouchy Logan, begrudgingly accept. From there, Mystique asks a series of questions about Wolverine’s past, and I decide the answers based on whether I choose to take a drink. Besides offering an unexpected degree of narrative agency in an otherwise linear action-adventure game, I was impressed by the level of nuance here. When I respond affirmatively to Mystique’s question about whether I’d ever sacrificed to save someone I love, Wolverine hesitates, subtly bristling with discomfort before slowly picking up the glass and downing the whisky as if Magneto himself was bringing the weight of the world down on him.
It’s a simple scene, but it’s such an effective way, through stunningly lifelike animation and a remarkably subdued performance by Liam McIntyre, to let the player truly feel the lingering pain that haunts the immortal mutant. It says a lot without overtly spelling everything out for us.
“Our Wolverine is very vulnerable,” creative director Marcus Smith tells me. “Wolverine is constantly feeling like he’s being manipulated and fighting against it. And in this case, we always need moments where he can reflect, because his moral code is one [where] he questions everything along the way.”
In the case of this tender Mystique moment, Smith credits one of the game’s “amazing” writers, Lauren Mee, who also worked on Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, for the original pitch that she later hashed out with game designer Keith Nakamura.
“You’re given a challenge, which is, ‘We know this is a low beat of exploration, and we know that you want to have a personal conflict conversation,'” says Smith. “And that one, it just works so well. Because no matter what you choose, the sentiment is right. It feels good. And it’s giving player choice. I know people who are like, ‘I just don’t want my Wolverine to drink so much, so I’m just not going to drink and answer it.’ And it still plays out beautifully.”
During this Princess Bar section, you also have to speak to Sabretooth, who, in stark contrast to the reserved Mystique, ends up body slamming Wolverine after lamenting that he isn’t “who he used to be” after leaving and rejoining Team X. And in a separate scene, Walter Langowski — the astrophysicist who in the comics becomes Sasquatch, a member of Wolverine’s Canadian Alpha Flight team — tries to cheer up Logan by having him search his office for a vinyl of their favourite song. These are the kind of rich and insightful character interactions that defined Insomniac’s brilliant work on Spider-Man, and it was reassuring to see that they’re absolutely still here in full force, even with a character who occupies a much more brutal and hate-filled corner of this world.
But of course, you also want this violence to feel satisfying, and so far, I’m loving what Insomniac is doing on that front.
The best there is at what they do
Right off the bat, Insomniac has opted for a third-person close-up view of Wolverine, giving the game a nice intimate feeling to enhance the brutality of combat à la modern God of War games. Every elegantly animated slash of his claws, every rugged, almost bear-like shuffle to the side as he dodges, every stylish crash zoom that punctuates fatal finishers — it all feels that much gnarlier with the camera hanging almost uncomfortably near Wolverine.
But I also appreciated how the flow of combat felt markedly different to Spider-Man. Where the Web-Head’s significant agility allowed for faster traversal, more seamless dodges and ground-to-aerial transitions, Logan has to worry more about situational awareness. In particular, he can do a feral pounce at a distant enemy, but that’s not always advised when they cluster together and one has a deadly shotgun or another an electrified melee weapon. On the flip side, Wolverine can use a powerful kick to either knock enemies into walls to stun them or even punt them off ledges entirely. And of course, there are parries you can perform, and some perfectly timed ones can even carry out cheer-worthy executions.
This creates a balletic rhythm to combat, as you can’t just wail on the nearest enemy and have to instead evaluate on the fly where to direct your fury. This was particularly noteworthy in a sequence in a makeshift town created by the villainous Bolivar Trask for one of his sadistic experiments. Some of the interiors of the houses felt almost claustrophobic compared to the preceding jungle environments, and it challenged me to be a bit more cautious accordingly.
I also appreciated how Insomniac incorporated Wolverine’s signature healing ability. While it works rather rapidly outside of combat, it recharges much more slowly mid-battle. What’s more, it feeds into a tiered Rage mechanic that charges the more Logan inflicts damage. Once you’ve filled enough of it, you can go into a Berserker state for visceral executions as the world seeps into a striking red-and-black colour palette. Having enough Rage is the only way to survive otherwise fatal attacks, as they’ll trigger Wolverine’s Last Stand mechanic, which lets him force himself back to his feet to revive, even as his metallic skeleton pokes through eviscerated pieces of skin. It’s a smart system that rewards you with a second chance by being aggressive, which fits with Wolverine’s fighting style.
“In earlier incarnations, we were doing sort of a more standard health increase. But what people were doing was you go away from combat to heal up, and so the model that we fell on was, “How do we promote the ‘always moving forward’ nature of Wolverine?” says Smith. “And that’s how you gain your rage, and that’s how you are preventing yourself from losing health by way of being able to trade the rage in for health in the Last Stand. It all just comes back to, “How do we make a game that actually has stakes with a character that is almost invulnerable?”
At the same time, Insomniac has found a clever way to factor in Wolverine’s heightened animalistic senses, especially in stealth. In the aforementioned fake town where you have to skulk around to find and destroy some of Trask’s generators, Wolverine can get visual wavelength cues towards the machines and ethereal blue highlights of the skeletons of enemies. It enhances the feeling of Wolverine being this bestial predator but in a more natural aesthetic way, rather than an overbearing UI element.
“It’s really hard not to make that overwhelming or just make it a ‘detective mode’ that you’re all used to where I’m going to hit this button. There are certain games that I won’t talk about where I spend all my time spamming because that’s a better view,” says Smith. “So we built all of the different incarnations, making it a passive element that’s more based on camera movement and what you’re focusing on. I think that’s the turning point where it felt unique to this game, and it felt like it wasn’t overwhelming.”
And finally, there’s the superhero setpieces you’ve come to expect. Of course, Insomniac’s Spider-Man delivered those in spades, with many sequences involving Spidey seamlessly navigating streets, skies and buildings as he fights his foes. But of course, Wolverine is comparatively much more grounded, with his game being set in a linear world instead of an open one.
“Obviously, Spider-Man moves very fast, and Wolverine does not move very fast. And so that meant creating something that’s much more intimate, having a lot more detail on local characters and environment, cameras a lot more moved in — just areas of focus that were different,” says Smith.
A key example of that was a standout fight against a half-finished Sentinel, which Trask intriguingly said in my demo was an expanded version from one seen in a previous mission set in Vancouver. [link to Canadian news story] Even without legs, this towering robot kept me on my toes with earth-shattering ground pounds, scorching lasers and barrages of missiles. With a lot of running, jumping and dodging alongside the help of Mystique and eventually Sabretooth, I was able to beat the machine, and it was an absolute blast.
Equally thrilling is a chase through Madripoor when The Hand ninja clan kidnaps Walter. Leaping over railings, building gaps and onto ziplines as the bustling markets teem with nightlife below us works just as well as any Spider-Man setpiece. And when I have to stop to fight some of The Hand, I’m taken aback by how refreshingly different they are to fight than Trask’s high-tech armada. With their fluid acrobatics, precise projectiles and special blades that can pierce Wolverine and temporarily stunt his healing, there’s an exceptional level of deadly tension as I fight them. All in all, it’s the level of tight and inventive game design that Insomniac brought to Spider-Man, but with an added layer of glorious brutality.
Final thoughts
By and large, I was really impressed with my demo. I expected the combat to be fast and hard-hitting, but all of the little nuances in terms of positioning and managing your Rage made it even better than I expected. All the while, I found myself connecting with Logan thanks to some wonderful storytelling choices that humanize him, especially in the moments outside of battle.
If I have any gripes so far, it’s that the optional Nightmare Doors that you can find, while offering worthwhile challenges centred around platforming and combat, feel a bit uninspired in that the insights into Wolverine’s past that they provide are relegated to narrated text.
It’s also hard to say how the overarching narrative will pan out, given the mysterious role of famed X-Men villain Mr. Sinister. In the demo, he’s only ever referred to by his civilian name, Nathaniel Essex, with his larger role of being the leader of Team X only briefly shown. It calls to mind how Marvel’s Spider-Man shocked us with Otto Octavius, who had been hidden from the marketing, by building him up as Peter’s friend and mentor to make his inevitable villainous turn as Dr. Octavius all the more resonant. Hopefully, Marvel’s Wolverine can do something similarly subversive with Essex despite lacking the element of surprise this time around.
Otherwise, I’m much more excited than I already was for Marvel’s Wolverine. With shared DNA with the Marvel’s Spider-Man series as many of its own meaningful narrative, gameplay and structural flourishes, this could very well be the Wolverine game of our dreams.
Marvel’s Wolverine launches exclusively on PS5 on September 15. For more on the game, check out our full interview with Smith.

articles.title: PBS broadcaster loses access to 50TB of data comprising 70 years of TV history after contracted cloud storage vendor goes defunct — public TV channel sues Iron Mountain data center, which hosts archival materials, to ensure preservation
articles.text:
PBS broadcaster loses access to 50TB of data comprising 70 years of TV history after contracted cloud storage vendor goes defunct — public TV channel sues Iron Mountain data center, which hosts archival materials, to ensure preservation
This wouldn't have been an issue if the organization bought a $1,000 NAS and populated it with a few hard drives.
Nine PBS is afraid that it will lose over 70 years of archival materials and programming after its contracted cloud storage vendor has apparently gone out of business. According to Current, the channel used Open Source Storage, or OSS, for storing over 50TB of data — but it suddenly lost access to its data earlier this year. Nine PBS has been working with OSS and its predecessor since 2019 and intended to renew its contract on March 6 of this year. The company never responded and abruptly cut off the station’s data access even though it still had 30 days to retrieve its data after the contract ended.
The station dug a little bit deeper when it discovered that the OSS website no longer existed and was listed as delinquent under the Colorado Secretary of State. It also discovered that OSS utilized Iron Mountain’s services, so it sent a demand letter to the latter to preserve its data and to "pay any reasonable costs associated with its demand." At the time, Iron Mountain did not confirm or deny that it possessed Nine PBS’ data.
At the same time, the channel also sued OSS and its leadership, which it paused after someone who claimed to be a "managing partner of the group that officially acquired" the company reached out. The person, named James Tramel, initially communicated with Nine PBS for about a month. However, this also ended abruptly, with the channel eventually receiving an automated reply from Tramel stating he is no longer connected with OSS. The channel was able to get in touch with him, and he said that he had "been defrauded" into acquiring the cloud storage company and that ownership and operations have now reverted to the previous owners.
This left the channel at a loss, so it continued its case against OSS, and the court ruled that Nine PBS had all the rights to access its data stored with OSS and that the latter should "facilitate its transfer to a new vendor." The channel’s attorney also reached out to Iron Mountain to inform the company of the pending case in Colorado; Iron Mountain finally admitted to holding the data. Iron Mountain initially agreed to turn over Nine PBS’ data, but it eventually backtracked and claimed that OSS owned the data it stored. Because of this, Nine PBS now has no choice but to sue Iron Mountain, too, to ensure the data is not deleted.
The entire thing is a nightmare scenario for Nine PBS, especially as it’s still unclear what will happen to its data. The channel can only assume that its former cloud storage provider is no longer paying data center bills, so it’s rightfully concerned that its data might end up lost forever. And even if Iron Mountain is willing to give Nine PBS its data, it risks getting sued by OSS — it is simply protecting itself by refusing to turn over the said stored data.
It seems that the safest legal way to resolve this issue is for Nine PBS to get a court order requiring Iron Mountain to turn over its data. But the channel must act quickly to ensure that its data, which Nine PBS VP and CCO Leah Freeman said to Current represented "70 years of our organization’s history," stays safe.
It's not clear if the channel has backups of its data, but based on its determination, we suspect not. This is strange, though, especially for a major organization, as one can easily purchase a six-bay NAS on Amazon and populate it with the best HDDs. This also goes against the 3-2-1 backup rule, which says you should keep three copies of your files stored in two different mediums, with one of them running offsite. Hopefully Nine PBS will implement a better backup system once it regains access to its data. And at least there's still a chance — it's not like the fire that the South Korean government experienced last year, which saw 858TB of data go up in smoke.

articles.title: OpenAI is losing its second executive this week
articles.text:
Another OpenAI executive is departing. Denise Dresser, who joined OpenAI as its chief revenue officer in December after serving as CEO of Slack, will be leaving in the “coming weeks” to “pursue other opportunities,” she said in a team note posted to LinkedIn. Dali Rajic, president and COO of Wiz, will be taking over the CRO role, OpenAI says.
OpenAI is losing its second executive this week
Chief revenue officer Denise Dresser announced she is leaving OpenAI. Two days ago, Brad Lightcap also said he’d be leaving.
Dresser’s departure is just the latest in a string of major exits. Earlier this week, special projects lead and former COO Brad Lightcap announced he would be leaving. (Dresser had taken over some of Lightcap’s work when he moved to the special projects role.) Former AGI chief Fidji Simo and former CMO Kate Rouch also recently stepped down.
“We’re now at an inflection point: the next generation of models will change not just how work gets done but how companies are built and run,” OpenAI says. “Dali will build the revenue operating system needed to scale for this next phase.”
Dresser is also leaving ahead of OpenAI’s IPO; the company announced in June that it had submitted a confidential S-1 filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission.

articles.title: Nvidia's new $500B plan is risky but brilliant, especially for aging GPUs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Nvidia announced this week that Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR were willing to commit up to $500 billion to build AI data centers. That eye-popping figure got a lot of the attention, but the bigger story is Nvidia’s effort to create a secondary market for aging GPUs.
To convince those big-name financial companies, Nvidia has agreed to guarantee, with its own money, that its chips used as collateral in these deals will retain their value.
Many have now commented on how unusual, smart, and dangerous this plan is. It is all of those things. The bond markets got so spooked that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang took to X and business TV to better explain how Nvidia’s risk would be limited.
But underneath the financial maneuvering to fund AI data centers (and keep revenue for Nvidia flowing), is something, perhaps, far more interesting for startups and enterprises: Huang wants to ensure an ecosystem of used AI hardware flourishes, helping sustain demand for Nvidia hardware as it ages.
Specifically, Nvidia is promising that if GPUs used as collateral don’t retain their value as expected, the company will cover up to 25% of the difference. So, if a data center owner defaults on a loan and the lender must liquidate, but the chips can’t command the price the books say they should, Nvidia will chip in.
The dangerous part for Nvidia is that this creates something financiers call “wrong way” risk. That is, Nvidia’s obligations will grow as demand weakens. Should that happen, its revenues will likely be squeezed as well.
Still, the scheme is deliberately unlike the comparison to Lucent Technologies that some have been making. Lucent was the telecommunications equipment provider that rose and crashed with the dotcom bubble after lending its customers money to buy its wares.
The Lucent comparison is a shadow over Nvidia, Huang knows. And not an unfair one. Nvidia definitely has committed billions toward those who buy its chips, including frontier AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic, neoclouds like CoreWeave (the originator of using Nvidia chips as collateral), as well as Nebius, Firmus, and Lambda. And it has been working on another $750 billion worth of circular deals this summer, Bloomberg has calculated.
“Is this circular financing?” Huang wrote on X about the new scheme. “This initiative is designed to address that concern. We are bringing independent, long-term institutional capital into the AI infrastructure market.”
That’s true. Unlike Lucent, Nvidia is getting others to shoulder the bulk of the capital and risk, merely by agreeing to protect a portion of its chips’ value in the future.
Should this plan work, Nvidia will have found new sources of money for AI data center builds, after many of the traditional methods have begun to wear thin. For instance, some of the hyperscalers have already taken on a lot of debt (like Oracle), issued new tranches of equity (Google), and burned much cash (Meta).
The situation has become so dicey that Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella recently recommended the book “1873” during his latest earnings call. It’s about the railroad-era financial engineering that crashed the nation’s economy.
The risk is that today’s AI boom, where demand far outstrips capacity, doesn’t continue for much longer. Rather than being in the early innings, what if enterprises and consumers temper AI usage? Or new technologies come along to make existing infrastructure more effective and/or all of today’s AI infrastructure obsolete?
Then, like so many buggy whips in the face of automobiles (to paraphrase Danny Devito’s Lawrence Garfield), demand dries up and everything crashes.
Yet, Huang is arguing that won’t happen by selling a vision of AI as a long-term “investable infrastructure,” as he describes it. That makes his AI servers, which he calls “AI factories” akin to railroads or airlines rather than quickly depreciating assets like PCs.
“When needs change, the factory can be used by another customer, another cloud or another operator. This broad ecosystem gives NVIDIA compute a deep market of potential users and offtakers, helping protect residual value,” he promised.
In that future, Nvidia cares as much about aging architecture as it does the new chips. And perhaps startups, enterprises, and even researchers will tap into a broader variety of hardware, each tuned to different AI needs, just like they are beginning to pick affordable open-weight models alongside the frontier choices.
As the king of AI, Nvidia has the power, and the window of opportunity, to make that happen.

articles.title: Building a practical path to post-quantum cryptography
articles.text:
Sponsored
Building a practical path to post-quantum cryptography
Quantum computing will reshape encryption, but not overnight, and a disciplined, phased approach lets organizations modernize cryptographic foundations without disruption while strengthening security today.
Provided byIntel
Quantum computing has alternated between breakthrough darling and overhyped promise in technology circles. Its powerful new capabilities come with a threat to break current cryptography, but for business leaders navigating the noise, the signal should be clear: post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is a manageable evolution, not a crisis.
The mathematics behind today's encrypted digital transactions may yield to quantum computers one day, but the transition to quantum-resistant algorithms is neither sudden nor insurmountable. For executives concerned about disruption, cost, or complexity, a structured and phased approach exists with trusted technology partners like Intel that are already beginning to deliver the infrastructure to make it possible.
A natural evolution, not a cliff edge
The "quantum threat" narrative often swings between two extremes: imminent catastrophe or distant irrelevance. The reality occupies a more pragmatic middle ground. Quantum computers are highly specialized accelerators that exploit quantum physics to solve specific hard problems. They have the potential to crack modern encryption, but they will not replace classic servers overnight, nor will they instantly break every encryption protocol on the internet. What they will do is gradually shift the security landscape, much as previous cryptographic transitions have done over the past three decades.
In late 2024, the Global Risk Institute, a Toronto-based financial services think tank, surveyed 32 quantum computing experts on when a quantum computer could break a 2048-bit RSA key within 24 hours. An average of optimistic and pessimistic estimates from the experts gave it an even 50-50 probability of reaching this code-breaking milestone by 2040. This timeline, uncertain but measurable, creates space for deliberate planning rather than emergency reaction. The near-term focus should be on "harvest now, decrypt later" scenarios, where adversaries collect encrypted data today and then hold it for future decryption later when that capability becomes possible. This is particularly applicable for information requiring confidentiality beyond 10 years.
For most enterprises, this can be a manageable risk when addressed through methodical modernization.
Government signals as confidence builders
The U.S. government has issued new directives for National Security Systems (NSS), which would likely be first on the list for potential quantum attack. Beginning in January 2027, new NSS acquisitions must be capable of supporting Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 2.0 (CNSA 2.0) requirements for PQC algorithms standardized by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and selected by the National Security Agency, the U.S. intelligence agency responsible for signals intelligence and information assurance. Implementation for new systems (with certain exceptions) is then required by 2031, with 100% adoption targeted by 2035.
For commercial enterprises, these timelines are not mandates, but could be signposts. They indicate where vendors, standards bodies, and auditors are headed, providing a reference architecture for responsible stewardship. Organizations can borrow this discipline without necessarily copying the exact timelines, using government guidance to calibrate their own risk tolerance and investment cadence.
Intel's role: Infrastructure ready for the transition
Intel is at the heart of the AI revolution by delivering quantum-resistant capabilities across our product portfolio. This is not just aspirational roadmap language; it is starting to be shipping technology.
For instance, the Intel Xeon 6 Processor already incorporates quantum-safe memory encryption (AES-256) and microcode signing to protect processor integrity. Upcoming platforms will extend post-quantum algorithms to more firmware and software signing, device interconnects, attestations, and secure boot functions, aligning with the most stringent government and industry directives.
Post-quantum algorithms carry different key sizes and computational overhead than legacy methods. Intel addresses this through dedicated cryptographic accelerators, optimized libraries, and specialized CPU instructions that reduce latency and preserve service-level agreements. Technologies such as Intel QuickAssist Technology offload cryptographic workloads, enabling enterprises to adopt stronger algorithms without sacrificing performance.
PQC is not a processor-alone problem. System builders and application owners must take a comprehensive view spanning solid-state drives, network interface cards, operating systems, hypervisors, applications, and connected services. Intel is delivering its pieces of the stack, while collaborating with ecosystem partners to ensure interoperability and smooth transition paths.
A more in-depth discussion of post-quantum algorithms and attacks can be found in my recent blog posted on Intel’s Community forum: "Post-Quantum Crypto: Panic Like It's 1999?"
A practical roadmap for enterprises
The path forward does not require upheaval, just discipline. Organizations can follow a phased approach that mirrors patterns emerging in government and critical infrastructure sectors:
- Approach PQC as modernization, not mitigation. Frame the transition as an opportunity to strengthen cryptographic foundations, reduce technical debt, and improve system maintainability.
- Leverage trusted partners. Technology suppliers like Intel are already shipping quantum-resistant capabilities with performance acceleration. Evaluate platform readiness and vendor roadmaps as part of procurement decisions.
- Start with visibility. Cryptography is embedded throughout modern technology stacks: not just in database encryption settings but in data at rest, data in transit, digital signatures, code signing, device identity, password hashing, and software update mechanisms. Start by mapping where cryptographic assets live, what algorithms protect them, and which data sets have the longest confidentiality requirements.
- Protect long-lived data first. Not all cryptographic uses age at the same rate. Encryption protecting long-lifespan intellectual property, personal data, or state secrets faces more immediate attention than short-lived session keys or rotating certificates. Focus initial investments on high-value, long-retention data stores and the trust anchors (root certificates, firmware signing keys) that underpin system integrity.
- Design for evolution and agility. Post-quantum algorithms are not simple drop-in replacements. They carry different key sizes, performance characteristics, and integration requirements that ripple through protocols, APIs, and hardware. Design systems that can transition algorithms without business disruption: testing compatibility, ensuring vendor roadmaps align, and engineering for rotation.
The bottom line
Quantum computing will reshape cryptography, but despite what occasional click-bait headlines say, it will not upend business overnight. The transition to post-quantum algorithms is a measured, multi-year journey, one that organizations can navigate with confidence by partnering with capable technology providers, prioritizing long-lived data, and designing for agility. Leaders who approach this as an engineering evolution rather than a threat response will not only be ready for whatever timeline quantum delivers; they will emerge with more robust, transparent, and maintainable cryptographic foundations across their platforms.

articles.title: WhatsApp estrena una función que detecta mensajes de estafa y te alerta antes de responder
articles.text:
WhatsApp está probando una nueva barrera que busca impedir las estafas que circulan por chat todos los días. Conocida como Scam Alert, esta función analiza los mensajes sin salir del teléfono para saber si puede ser fraudulento. Meta promete que esta característica no viola la privacidad de los usuarios ni el cifrado de extremo a extremo.
De acuerdo con una publicación en su web de ingeniería, WhatsApp comenzó a probar la herramienta con un grupo limitado de usuarios. Scam Alert utiliza un modelo de aprendizaje automático que se ejecuta directamente en el móvil, por lo que no es necesario enviar los mensajes a servidores externos para analizarlos.
El sistema analiza los mensajes que llegan de números que no se encuentran en tu lista de contactos. Scam Alert revisa el contenido para identificar ciertas características, como la estructura de la conversación y señales en el lenguaje. En caso de que detecte patrones que coincidan con estafas conocidas, lanzará una advertencia dentro del chat que solo tú podrás ver.
Ante la preocupación de que Meta pueda leer tus chats, la compañía aseguró que ningún contenido de los mensajes sale del teléfono para ser analizado. Una vez que activas la función, WhatsApp descargará el modelo de IA para que el análisis se lleve a cabo en el dispositivo. Los chats nunca se subirán a un servidor de Meta o de terceros, por lo que puedes estar seguro de que tu información se encuentra a salvo.
Scam Alert es completamente opcional y puede activarse o desactivarse cuando quieras desde los ajustes de WhatsApp. En caso de que recibas una advertencia que se generó por error, existe una opción para marcar la conversación como confiable y evitar que el sistema la analice a futuro. De igual modo, es posible compartir los últimos cinco mensajes recibidos para ayudar a mejorar la precisión del modelo, aunque esto será voluntario.
Cómo funciona Scam Alert, la nueva función de WhatsApp para prevenir estafas
En su análisis técnico, Meta señala que construyó Scam Alert sobre tres principios para mantener la coherencia del cifrado de extremo a extremo. El primero establece que, tanto el modelo como los datos que procesa, permanecen siempre en el dispositivo. El segundo impide que la empresa envíe reportes automáticos de los mensajes o alertas, mientras que el tercero tiene que ver con el control de desactivarla cuando desees.
Para garantizar la privacidad del usuario, WhatsApp diseñó varios mecanismos de verificación. La telemetría que se recopila se procesa dentro de un entorno confidencial antes de convertirse en datos anónimos.
Por último, Meta dice que no puede entregar una versión específica del modelo a un usuario en particular. Cada versión, incluidas las experimentales, se publica antes en un registro de transparencia público. La tecnológica añadió que tienen pensado publicar los pesos del modelo para que investigadores de seguridad puedan auditarlo y comprobar que se desarrolló con el fin de frenar las estafas.
Por ahora, Scam Alert estará disponible en fase beta con un grupo de usuarios y miembros de la comunidad que identifica vulnerabilidades. WhatsApp no reveló cuándo se lanzará a todo el público, ya que primero tiene que asegurarse de que funciona y cumple con los requerimientos de privacidad y seguridad.

articles.title: Alabama residents left powerless to stop massive Bitcoin mining data center despite county and town moratoriums — hole in state zoning laws lets facility through
articles.text:
Alabama residents left powerless to stop massive Bitcoin mining data center despite county and town moratoriums — hole in state zoning laws lets facility through
Public pressure mounts on data center buildouts in Alabama.
Somerville in Morgan County, Alabama, is a quiet, idyllic town full of green pastures, grazing animals, and soon enough, a Bitcoin mining center. Despite the many protests from residents and moratoriums at both county and town level, the 50-MW facility from VoltCore is going ahead, due to a teeny weeny problem with the zoning laws: there aren't any, or at least, none that apply.
More specifically, Alabama is one of the many states where counties don't have any power over zoning (Dillon's Rule) until they hit at least 600,000 residents, which isn't the case in Morgan County. Municipalities and towns do have that legal ability, but many towns don't apply it, and when they do, they have limitations on how they apply it outside of town borders. That's precisely the situation that Somerville and its residents find themselves in, having had no need for zoning control until now.
Both the county and Somerville have enacted moratoriums against VoltCore's buildout, but those cannot legally stop the construction, since it's built on private land. According to Ray Long, Morgan County Commission Chairman, "We can’t keep them from doing anything right now because there's no laws at all in Morgan County in rural areas [...] There's no zoning, there’s none of that, so we really don't have anything to stand on other than what we can say is, 'We really wish you wouldn't do it.'"
There are also several petitions running, the largest with about 2,000 signatories, and a GoFundMe campaign to try and hire a lawyer to help with the situation. Alabama's Limited Self-Governance Act does predict having to deal with noise and pollution concerns, but it's written in such a way that specifically prevents it from being used to control zoning. The VoltCore build even has an approved energy connection from the Tennessee Valley Authority, and work is reportedly proceeding as usual, connecting water, gas, and AT&T lines.
Even if the Somerville town drafted a local law for zoning, it would take many months and multiple rounds for it to pass, and even still would almost certainly only apply prospectively and not to the VoltCore installation. Furthermore, the data center's location just outside the edge of town could put it outside legal reach regardless.
Other Alabama counties have taken notice of the problem, though, as a recent report indicates that data center bans will be a hot topic at an upcoming Association of County Commissioners. The dim view of data centers in general across the United States has rallied quite a number of states. South Dakota signed a law limiting installations of 10 MW or more, while New York, Oklahoma, North Carolina, and many others all have proposals in motion to hold or control new buildouts.

articles.title: Claude Cowork is coming to your Chrome browser, and I might finally use it now
articles.text:
Claude Cowork is coming to your Chrome browser, and I might finally use it now
Get extra input on your work tasks with Claude Cowork in Chrome
- Claude Cowork is coming to Google Chrome side panels
- Claude can now connect across multiple systems and tools
- Users will start seeing the upgrade now
Anthropic has revealed it is upgrading the Claude in Chrome browser extension tool into a fully-fledged AI-powered work assistant.
The tool, designed as a side panel, will now be a Claude Cowork session, allowing users to access the company's AI tools in the browser to help crack those tricky work tasks.
"Conversations are saved to your history, your skills and connectors work in the browser, and a task you start in a tab can be finished on the Claude desktop, web, and mobile apps," Anthropic noted in a blog post announcing the news.
Cowork in Chrome
The company notes that while many of the tools that users interact with each day are already connected to Claude, others such as internal dashboards, legacy systems, and vendor portals are not.
This therefore needed a separate side panel session, which could interrupt workflows for some workers.
Connecting these via the new addition will mean that Claude can work in these apps through the Chrome browser, carrying context and conversations across your vital tools, whether that's on desktop, web or mobile.
Anthropic says the side panel will run the same Claude Cowork session being used for longer, multi-step work, such as creating a budget spreadsheet that needs to pull in invoices from multiple vendor portals.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Claude in Chrome would be able to gather up the amounts and dates needed before building the spreadsheet, allowing you to continue the session in the desktop app to add files from your computer, or import last month's budget and ask what's changed, allowing you to maintain context across surfaces as you work.
And because sessions live with your account rather than a single device, you can start work in a browser and pick it up later somewhere else.
Anthropic has also moved to address growing concerns around prompt injection cyberattacks against agents such as Claude in Chrome by adding a step where the tool will ask for a check from the user before carrying out any major action, such as submitting a form, sending a message, or downloading a file.
Users on a Max and Team plans will see the change immediately, or can install the extension from the Chrome Web Store now - it will be rolling out to Pro users over the coming weeks.

articles.title: Instagram se marca un 'Jaguar' con un cambio de logotipo que nadie pidió
articles.text:
Por alguna razón, Instagram acaba de cambiar su icónico logotipo después de una década. La versión en letra cursiva, fácilmente identificable y conocida por todos, será reemplazada por una opción que ya está generando polémica. En cierto modo incluso recuerda al episodio de Jaguar, que a finales de 2024 generó gran controversia tras actualizar su logo e imagen de marca de forma inesperada.
En el caso de Instagram, el logotipo abandona la cursiva y adopta un formato en imprenta minúscula que busca ser más simple y limpio, pero que se siente casi tan genérico como el de Jaguar. Fue Adam Mosseri, jefe de la red social, el encargado de dar a conocer el nuevo diseño a través de sus cuentas personales.
Las respuestas de los usuarios parecen bastante divididas: o lo odian, o lo aman. Lo curioso es que tanto en Instagram como en Threads se repiten los comentarios apuntando a que la "r" se parece en realidad a una "z", dando la impresión de que en realidad dice "Instagzam". Es lógico pensar que será solo cuestión de minutos hasta que aparezcan los primeros memes en tal sentido.
"El logotipo en la parte superior de la aplicación no había cambiado en 10 años, así que era hora de renovarlo. Un diseño más limpio y moderno, con referencias al original y la sencillez y el cuidado que siempre han caracterizado a Instagram", publicó Mosseri. En Threads, en tanto, agregó que esperaba ver las opiniones fuertes o hot takes de sus seguidores. Además, allí también indicó que el logotipo de Instagram anterior se veía "anticuado".
Instagram actualiza su logotipo con un cambio polémico
Instagram está lejos de ser la primera empresa que cambia su logotipo después de varios años atada al mismo. Sin embargo, no deja de sentirse como un cambio innecesario. El cambio de tipografía elimina lo último que quedaba de la esencia original de la imagen de marca de la plataforma.
La versión actual en cursiva estaba vigente desde mayo de 2016. Y si bien no era la original, las modificaciones que se implementaron sobre el logotipo que Instagram usaba desde 2010 habían sido bastante sutiles. Ahora, Meta ha decidido borrar de un plumazo lo que quedaba de esa identidad. No olvidemos que la plataforma ya había quedado en el centro de una controversia cuando decidió eliminar el ícono de su app, eliminando la cámara y adoptando el que tenemos en la actualidad.
Ya veremos si los diseñadores de Meta hacen algún cambio en el logotipo de Instagram para corregir la "r" y evitar que lo de "Instagzam" se convierta en una pesadilla de marketing, o si optan por mantenerlo tal y como está. Una actualización que nadie pidió pero que muy pronto verás en tu móvil.

articles.title: I tried out the Centauri Carbon 2 as a total 3D printing noob: Here’s what I learned
articles.text:
3D printing has always appealed to me, but because of the associated unknowns, I have never really pulled the trigger. I’m sure I’m not alone.
Will I be able to set the printer up? Will the experience truly be plug-and-play? How will I design the things I want to print? Are there other associated costs?
Those are just some of the early questions that kept me away from seriously getting into the hobby.
My curiosity really piqued when I stumbled upon an Instagram account that shared short timelapse videos of Pokémon figurines being 3D printed. The account’s entire feed offered a look at vibrant figurines materializing layer by layer from the ground up.
I’m a sucker for figurines, and I, along with my housemates, have an entire cabinet dedicated to Funkos and such. The idea of designing and printing my own figurines to add to the collection pushed me closer than ever to finally take the plunge.
Then came the opportunity to spend some time with Elegoo’s Centauri Carbon 2, and, well, it made me realize that 3D printing has come a long way and is remarkably easy to get into. It also made me realize that social media has a way of hiding the less fabulous parts of any hobby. What looks like a seamless print actually involves several smaller decisions and learning points.
The printer isn’t really the problem. That’s actually the easiest part of 3D printing. Unboxing and setting up the Centauri Carbon 2 was a breeze.
I had expected a gruelling setup process, but that wasn’t the case. The factory folks did most of the heavy lifting here.
Once the initial calibration process and the obligatory Benchy (a standard test print) were out of the way, I ran into my first real issue: even the most beginner-friendly printer needs to be told what to print.
What to print?
Elegoo includes a USB stick with the Centauri Carbon 2 that has a few basic designs, which gave me an easy way to get my feet wet. But those models will only get you so far.
That’s when I realized that figuring out what to print is a hobby by itself.
You could go the designing route and learn software like Tinkercad, Onshape, or Blender. There’s a learning curve there, but the payoff is ultimately very rewarding, especially when you get to see your own idea come to life.
Learning to design, however, takes time. That’s where online repositories and 3D printing communities come in.
MakerWorld is one of the biggest options, but alternatives like Printables, Thingiverse, Nexprint, and more are equally valuable resources for beginners. Said websites offer thousands of pre-designed files created by other users. You either browse around until you see something that interests you, or you search for a specific idea already in mind. I’m a huge soccer fan, so I had to print these jersey designs as soon as I saw them on MakerWorld:
Then comes the slicer
You still can’t simply hit print though. Once you’ve decided what you want to print, you still need to prepare the file for printing. This is where slicers come in.
Slicers come in all shapes and sizes, but I, up until now, have only relied on Elegoo’s own slicer. For beginners, this is where things actually start to feel a little intimidating.
Think of slicers as the middlemen between designs and your printer. This is where your design (or the design that you found online) is broken down into thousands of individual layers, turning it into instructions that your printer can actually understand and print.
Slicers can be difficult to understand, but that’s only if you get into the intricacies of it. For a beginner, simply slicing a design and making minor placement or size-related changes is a relatively seamless process.
This is also where you’ll get an estimate of how long your print will take (more on that later) and how much filament it will take up – this leads me to the next main concern that crisp timelapses on social media do not show you.
Failed prints and wasted filament
Things will go wrong, and sometimes, that’ll be right when you walk away.
You could be monitoring your print and see its first few layers come out absolutely fine. You think that’s great and go about your day only to find a spaghettified mess hours later. That truly sucks, not just because of the wasted filament or because of the time taken. It’s the anticipation of seeing the design eventually come to life, only for the excitement to be delayed by a failure that could have been avoided.
Failed prints, however, are part of the learning experience. For example, after a few of my prints failed back-to-back, I researched and learned that the base plate could become oily from contact with my fingers. This was causing adhesion issues where the first layer of the print wasn’t properly sticking to the base plate. Wiping the plate down with isopropyl alcohol solved the problem. Now, I’ve made a habit of proactively wiping down the plate after a few prints.
On that note, failed prints aren’t the only way you can end up wasting a lot of filament. There’s another source of filament waste, and this one truly surprised me. Printing in multiple colours at once, even when your print goes right, will eat up your spool.
The Centauri Carbon 2 has a Canvas system that allows it to swap between four filament spools. This is incredibly useful if you’re printing something that has multiple colours. However, there is a catch. Each time that the printer switches to a different spool, it first has to purge the remaining filament from the previous colour before feeding in the new one. This is done to ensure no mixup of colours.
When a model requires frequent colour changes, this purge, or as the community likes to call it, Printer Poop, can be substantial. This, on the Centauri Carbon 2, shoots out from the proverbial rear.
With several of my prints, the amount wasted on printer purge was more than the amount of filament that actually went into the print. That’s the tradeoff that comes with being able to print in colour. That immediately changed when I realized that some designs don’t need to be printed in multiple colours at once. Instead, I could split my model into different parts, print each part separately in the required colour, and then put everything together afterward.
This approach, of course, is more work, but it significantly cuts down on the filament wasted.
Prints take time, more than you might have expected
Okay, so you’ve calibrated your printer, ironed out the initial kinks, and have found a design that’s all sliced up and ready to be printed. You glance at the estimated time the print is expected to take, and it’s in hours. Double-digits too.
You soon learn about another reality of 3D printing: printing takes a lot of time.
A small Pokémon figurine that looks relatively simple on your computer screen can take several hours to be printed. The Pikachu I referenced earlier took a little over 6 hours to print. The Cactus toothpick holder took a little under eight hours.
Larger prints that often make the rounds online can easily take over 24 hours of constant print time to materialize. And if things go wrong near the end of a long print, you’ve essentially wasted an entire day’s worth of printing time and filament.
It’s helpful that the Centauri Carbon 2 has a built-in camera that faces the base plate. It allows me to monitor the print remotely from the slicer instead of having to constantly walk over to the printer to check whether everything is going according to plan. It’s a great quality-of-life feature that I can see being useful regardless of whether you’re a complete beginner or a 3D printing veteran. More importantly, remotely monitoring your prints can also help save filament.
In scenarios where my print begins failing for any reason, monitoring via the camera allows me to catch the problem early and stop the print before too much filament is wasted on something that was never going to turn out as intended.
That pretty much sums up my short-term experience with the 3D printing and the Centauri Carbon 2. The printer has given me the occasional error, but nothing that a little troubleshooting doesn’t fix. Oh, and that isn’t unique to the Centauri Carbon 2. From what I’ve learned, troubleshooting errors is simply a not-so-fun part of 3D printing, regardless of which printer you use.
I’m still very much a beginner, and there’s a lot more that I need to learn. I haven’t yet experimented with different filament types, textured base plates, nozzle sizes, advanced slicer settings, and more. Expect a much deeper dive into 3D printing and the Centauri Carbon 2 once I have more experience under my belt.

articles.title: DeepSeek open sources an agent harness where everything is a plugin
articles.text:
DeepSeek open sources an agent harness where everything is a plugin
DeepSeek on Thursday open sourced the DeepSeek Harness, a new agent runtime for developers.
The Node.js-based harness is now available on GitHub as a developer preview and under an MIT license.
Clearly, there is some interest in the new harness. Within only a few hours, the repo picked up more than 33,000 GitHub stars, and that number is climbing quickly. Theirs is already a thriving ecosystem of community plugins.
What sets the DeepSeek harness apart is that “everything is a plugin,” as DeepSeek puts it. And the team takes that quite literally. The model adapter, the tool registry, the session log, and the agent loop itself are all plugins — and each one is replaceable.
There’s “no privileged core to patch,” the project’s documentation notes, so extending the harness simply means mounting a plugin beside the others.
The overall architecture is based on Cordis, a “meta-framework for spatiotemporal composability.” To some degree, that sounds more complicated than it is. The core idea here is that software tools like modern AI harnesses require dynamic composition, meaning it needs to be easy to add and remove components without affecting the rest of the system — and those components need to be able to easily interact and understand how they depend on each other.
A recent paper by three researchers from Peking University and DeepSeek explains this in more detail and forms the basis of Cordis and the DeepSeek Harness.
Four modes, one model
The harness itself ships with four presets. Standard mode gives developers the full coding agent, with filesystem tools, shell access, web search capability, subagents, and a plan mode. On the other end, Minimal strips this down to only two tools, bash and str_replace_editor.
Then there is Code mode, which changes how tools reach the model. Rather than exposing those tools as individual function calls, it generates a TypeScript SDK and lets the model write a program against it, so a sequence that would otherwise take five round trips runs as a single call.
The fourth preset, Creator mode, is meant for developers who want to create custom agent presets. It inherits all of the features of the Standard mode and adds runtime inspection, plugin experiments, and preset-authoring guidance.
Everything the model sees gets logged
Another core feature of the harness is that it keeps an append-only session log. Anything that reaches a model request has to be reconstructable from that log.
This also means that the conversation history is not just an implementation detail. Instead, core features like resume, fork, replay, transcripts, telemetry, and the web UI are all based on this single event stream. Adding any new kind of model-visible input therefore means adding a new session event.
The agent sandboxing is similarly strict — as it should be for any agent harness. The local backend wraps subprocesses in Linux Landlock through a Node addon DeepSeek wrote, macOS Seatbelt, or a Windows ACL restricted-token runner.
Someone else’s model
It’s worth stressing that nothing in the harness ties it to DeepSeek’s models. Indeed, the provider catalog covers Anthropic, OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, Microsoft Azure and Google’s Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (though the documentation still calls it Vertex), alongside DeepSeek’s own endpoint. There is also the option to add custom OpenAI-compatible gateways for other inference providers.
What’s interesting is that the harness also ships with two subagent providers to delegate work directly to Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex, resolving each product’s binary from the host PATH so the user supplies the install and the login. Both ship switched off by default.
DeepSeek also ships bridges that run a user’s existing hooks.json from either product against the harness’s own interception points, which the README describes as a compatibility path rather than the better design.
There’s also an MCP client, Agent Client Protocol support, and the harness can read AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files.
No pull requests (yet)
As for contributing to the project, DeepSeek currently notes that “We are sorry that we cannot accept external pull requests at the moment.” Instead, it points would-be contributors to GitHub Discussions and to building plugins instead.
The company says it doesn’t consider packages in the official repository inherently more important than community ones, and that readers should treat the repo as “an idea, an official showcase, and a source of inspiration, but not a mandate from us.”
At this point, harnesses are everywhere, of course, and every major lab ships a coding agent now. Among the Chinese labs, Alibaba’s Qwen Code and ByteDance’s Trae Agent both launched in mid-2025, with Moonshot’s Kimi CLI following that October, and Zhipu’s ZCode arriving in July.
DeepSeek clearly believes that its plugin architecture is the major differentiator here, though, and while most of the competition is open source, the early reaction to the new harness shows that even though there’s plenty of competition, DeepSeek may have hit upon something here that developers are looking for.

articles.title: DJI Neo 2 : ce petit drone 4K avec son pack FPV et sa multitude d'accessoires vole sous les 500 € — Frandroid
articles.text:
En 2024, DJI avait frappé fort en lançant un minuscule drone grand public, le Neo, capable de filmer sans télécommande et de décoller depuis la main de l’utilisateur pour le suivre ensuite. Malgré ses grandes qualités, ce drone n’était pas exempt de défauts, mais DJI a corrigé les principaux points faibles de ce premier modèle. Le Neo 2 qui lui a succédé (et que l’on a noté 9/10) propose notamment un évitement d’obstacles bluffant, des images en 4K 60p et des capacités de suivi bien meilleures. Actuellement, cet excellent petit drone se trouve dans un pack très complet, avec notamment des lunettes FPV, à moins de 500 euros.
Les atouts de ce pack DJI Neo 2
- Un drone totalement autonome qui s’élève tout seul
- La qualité vidéo 4K 60p
- Des lunettes DJI Goggles N3 pour le piloter comme un drone FPV
Lancé à 579 euros, le pack DJI Neo 2 Motion Fly More Combo peut vous revenir à 469 euros chez Joybuy grâce au code promo MOTION valable jusqu’au 31 août 2026. Ce pack contient le drone, les lunettes DJI Goggles N3, la télécommande RC Motion 3, trois batteries de vol intelligentes, une station de recharge bidirectionnelle, une paire de protections d’hélices, un émetteur-récepteur numérique, des hélices de rechange, une protection de nacelle ou encore un câble USB-C vers USB-C.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le DJI Neo 2. Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
La FUJIKINA, c’est les 4, 5 et 6 septembre prochains ! Testez les produits Fujifilm et rencontrez les photographes invités. Votre billet d’entrée inclut le prêt de matériel, les sessions Touch & Try, le nettoyage de vos capteurs, des photowalks exclusifs ainsi que des studios démo accompagnés par des pro.
Un drone tout léger et bien plus armé pour gérer les obstacles
Le DJI Neo 2 conserve le format FPV inspiré de l’Avata 2 de la même marque, avec ses hélices entièrement carénées. Il fait partie des drones les plus légers du constructeur, même s’il est un poil plus lourd que son prédécesseur (151 g contre 135 g). Rassurez-vous, il se situe lui aussi dans la classe C0, laquelle dispense l’utilisateur de toute formation obligatoire. L’enregistrement du drone ou l’obtention d’un brevet d’aptitude de pilote à distance ne sont même pas requis.
S’il ressemble physiquement au premier DJI Neo, le DJI Neo 2 s’en démarque sur plusieurs points. Il arbore notamment deux antennes externes à l’arrière, qui améliorent la portée et la stabilité de la connexion quand on utilise le drone avec la télécommande. Ce n’est pas tout. Alors que le Neo se contentait de deux mini-caméras sur le ventre pour gérer son atterrissage, le Neo 2 se dote de deux caméras fish-eye qui lui servent à atterrir et à voir tout son environnement, ainsi que d’un capteur Lidar qui mesure la distance aux objets avec une grande précision.
C’est grâce à ces capteurs que le Neo 2 parvient à offrir une détection d’obstacles omnidirectionnelle franchement bluffante. Le premier Neo, lui, n’embarquait que des capteurs ventraux. Le drone gagne aussi un écran sur le flanc gauche, qui permet de choisir son plan et de faire décoller l’appareil sans utiliser son smartphone. Le drone peut ainsi partir de votre paume, vous reconnaître et commencer à filmer. À l’usage, c’est vraiment impressionnant.
La 4K 60p, enfin !
Le DJI Neo 2 est équipé, comme le modèle précédent, d’un capteur de 1/2 pouce. Mais alors que le Neo se limitait à la 4K 30p, le Neo 2 passe enfin à la 4K 60p. Les images filmées sont donc bien plus nettes et fluides. Notez toutefois que vous n’aurez pas accès aux modes « pro » réservés aux modèles plus premium de la marque : pas de D-Log, de HLG ni de mode RAW ici. Le Neo 2 vise donc l’efficacité plutôt que la post-production poussée. Il mise sur un format universel (SDR Rec.709) immédiatement exploitable pour un partage sur les réseaux sociaux. Les Mastershots (Dronie, Helix, Rocket) sont également disponibles pour vous permettre de réaliser très facilement des séquences courtes plus « pro ».
Le Neo 2 a par ailleurs été conçu pour voler de manière autonome et interagir avec vous grâce à des commandes gestuelles. Votre main devient en réalité une télécommande : déplacez votre paume vers la gauche, et le drone se décale à gauche. Notez également que les capacités de suivi du Neo 2 sont bien meilleures que celles du Neo, qui s’arrêtait beaucoup trop souvent au moindre obstacle. La stabilisation en vol a elle aussi été améliorée : le Neo 2 est doté d’une nacelle mécanique stabilisée sur deux axes (gimbal) couplée à sa stabilisation électronique RockSteady.
Côté performances en vol, il ne faut pas attendre de miracles d’un drone de 151 g. Ses moteurs sont certes plus puissants que ceux du Neo, mais le vent peut vite le ralentir. Enfin, côté autonomie, le Neo 2 est censé offrir 19 minutes, mais en pratique, il ne faut pas espérer plus de 12 à 13 minutes de vol utile. Heureusement, des batteries supplémentaires sont incluses dans le pack.
Pour en savoir encore plus, n’hésitez pas à lire notre test complet du DJI Neo 2.
Si vous souhaitez découvrir d’autres modèles que nous recommandons, nous vous invitons dès maintenant à consulter notre guide des meilleurs drones du moment.
